Measured on 2026-09-01 with scripts/verify-cert-expiry.sh on macOS 26.6.2 / OpenSSH_10.3p1.

Answer: an expired X.509 certificate does not affect this path. sc_auth sees the expiry and reports certificateValid=false, yet provider-backed signing, localhost authentication, and a fresh ssh-keygen -K identity-file download all still succeed. The replacement certificate came from an unrelated throwaway CA, so OpenSSH is not tolerating an expired certificate — it does not consult the certificate here at all.

Consequences: no warning is warranted, because certificate validity is not a signal about SSH usability and presenting it as one would mislead. No renewal workflow is warranted either. This also confirms the handoff's rule not to infer an identity is safe to delete because its certificate looks expired.

CSR and certificate replacement for the same non-exportable key work as documented: sc_auth create-ctk-csr followed by import-ctk-certificate leaves the key, its hashes, and its SSH fingerprint unchanged — proven by the identity file still passing the fingerprint preflight afterwards.

Recorded in docs/HARDWARE_VERIFICATION.md. Not covered: whether macOS itself expires or renews these certificates over time, and whether other Apple subsystems consuming CTK identities care. This measured OpenSSH.

Measured 2026-09-01 on macbookair-m1 (MacBook Air M1, macOS 26.6.2) and mac-studio-m1u (Mac Studio M1 Ultra, macOS 26.6.2).

unlocked: passed. locked: passed. logged-out: FAILED. pre-first-unlock: not attempted.

The logged-out failure is the significant result and its mechanism is specific: sc_auth still enumerates the identity, OpenSSH still loads the key and has the server accept it, and the provider still opens — but sk_sign returns -4, 'device not found'. The Secure Enclave token requires a console session. Locking the screen keeps it; logging out removes it.

Two findings came out of the same runs. sc_auth create-ctk-identity exits 0 and creates nothing while logged out, caught only because identity create compares the inventory before and after instead of trusting the exit status. And doctor reported an all-clear on a logged-out Mac where nothing could sign, because every check it made inspected a binary; it now reports the console session and warns when there is none.

pre-first-unlock stays not-run: FileVault makes it unreachable on this hardware, since the pre-boot authentication that starts the system is itself a login. Its outcome is strongly implied by the logged-out row but was not measured, and an implication is not a measurement.

Consequence, recorded in README.md and docs/THREAT_MODEL.md: the remote-Mac workflow -t none exists for works provided the account stays logged in at the console. That constraint cuts both ways — a Mac that must stay logged in, combined with -t none removing per-use approval, means any process running as that user can request signatures.
